hints: For P, look at the C=C bond and check if each carbon has two different groups attached, then decide if cis-trans isomerism is possible.
For Q, R and S, look for a carbon attached to four different groups and recall which type of stereoisomerism that allows.
walkthrough:
Check P for geometrical isomerism**
P is $\text{CH}_3\text{CH=CHCH}_3$ (but-2-ene). Each C of the C=C has two different groups, $\text{CH}_3$ and H, and rotation is restricted. So cis and trans forms exist. P has no carbon with four different groups, so no optical isomerism.

Check Q, R and S for a chiral centre**
Q is $\text{CH}_3\text{CHBrCH}_2\text{CH}_3$, R is $\text{CH}_3\text{CH}_2\text{CH(CH}_3\text{)CN}$ and S is $\text{CH}_3\text{CH}_2\text{CH(CH}_3\text{)COOH}$. In each, carbon 2 is bonded to H, $\text{CH}_3$, $\text{CH}_2\text{CH}_3$ and Br / CN / COOH. That is four different groups, so each has a chiral centre and shows optical isomerism. None has a C=C with two different groups on each carbon, so none shows geometrical isomerism.
Final answer: Geometrical isomerism: P tick only. Optical isomerism: Q, R, S tick only (P no tick).

hints: P is but-2-ene reacting with HBr, so think about where H and Br add across the C=C bond.
walkthrough:
Add HBr across the double bond**
Think of reaction 1 as breaking the pi bond in $\text{CH}_3\text{CH=CHCH}_3$ and adding H to one carbon and Br to the other. Because P is symmetrical, addition to either carbon gives the same product: $\text{CH}_3\text{CHBrCH}_2\text{CH}_3$. This is 2-bromobutane, which contains the chiral centre you spotted in part (a).

hints: In reaction 2 Br in Q is replaced by CN from KCN, so decide if CN- is acting as an electrophile or a nucleophile.
walkthrough:
Spot the substitution by a nucleophile**
In Q to R, $\text{-Br}$ is swapped for $\text{-CN}$. The reagent $\text{CN}^-$ from KCN in ethanol is a nucleophile with a lone pair that attacks the electron deficient carbon bonded to Br. So the mechanism is nucleophilic substitution.

hints: Reaction 3 converts $\text{-CN}$ to $\text{-COOH}$ using $\text{H}^+(aq)$, so think what small molecules must add to supply O and H.
walkthrough:
Balance the nitrile hydrolysis**
Picture $\text{R-CN}$ gaining two waters: the N ends up as $\text{NH}_4^+$ in acid and the carbon ends up as $\text{R-COOH}$. The balanced equation is $$\text{C}_4\text{H}_9\text{CN} + 2\text{H}_2\text{O} + \text{H}^+ \rightarrow \text{C}_4\text{H}_9\text{COOH} + \text{NH}_4^+$$ Check atoms and charge: both sides have the same C, H, O, N and +1 charge.

hints: Recall that the small [M+1]+ peak is mainly due to one $^{13}$C in the molecule, with about 1.1% abundance per carbon.
Set up the ratio of peak heights: ([M+1]+ / M+) x 100 gives the total % due to $^{13}$C, then divide by 1.1 to get number of carbons.
walkthrough:
Link the [M+1]+ height to carbon number**
Each carbon atom has about a 1.1% chance of being $^{13}$C. So a molecule with n carbons gives an [M+1]+ height about $n \times 1.1$% of the M+ height. That gives: $$n \times 1.1 = \frac{\text{abundance of [M+1]}^+}{\text{abundance of M}^+} \times 100$$

Substitute and calculate**
Put in the Table 4.2 values: $$n = \frac{0.55}{7.2} \times \frac{100}{1.1} = 6.94$$ This rounds to 7, so U contains 7 carbon atoms.
Final answer: number of C atoms $= \frac{0.55}{7.2} \times \frac{100}{1.1} = 6.94 \approx 7$

hints: Look for the very strong sharp dip near $1700 \text{ cm}^{-1}$ in Fig. 4.2 and match it to a bond in Table 4.3.
Check for a second strong absorption in the $1040-1300 \text{ cm}^{-1}$ fingerprint region and think which functional group needs both C=O and C-O together.
walkthrough:
Read the two key dips**
In Fig. 4.2 there is a very strong absorption at about $1730 \text{ cm}^{-1}$ and another strong set around $1100-1200 \text{ cm}^{-1}$. From Table 4.3, $1710-1750 \text{ cm}^{-1}$ is C=O in an ester and $1040-1300 \text{ cm}^{-1}$ is C-O in an ester or hydroxy compound.

Combine to identify ester**
A carboxylic acid would also have C=O and C-O, but it would show a very broad O-H band at $2500-3000 \text{ cm}^{-1}$ which is absent here. An alcohol would show O-H at $3200-3650 \text{ cm}^{-1}$ which is also absent. The combination of C=O plus C-O with no O-H and a single functional group in U points to ester, $\text{RCOOR'}$.

Final answer: functional group: ester
Absorption at $1710-1750 \text{ cm}^{-1}$ due to C=O stretch and absorption at $1040-1300 \text{ cm}^{-1}$ due to C-O stretch. Only ester contains both.

hints: S is a $\text{C}_5$ carboxylic acid reacting with alcohol T to give ester U plus water, so use the 7 carbons in U to find how many carbons T must supply.
With 2 carbons needed from T and only one functional group, think which simple alcohol fits, then join S and T by removing water.
walkthrough:
Work out T from the carbon balance**
S is $\text{CH}_3\text{CH}_2\text{CH(CH}_3\text{)COOH}$ which has 5 carbons. U has 7 carbons from (c)(i). Esterification is acid + alcohol to ester + water, with no carbons lost. So T must provide $7 - 5 = 2$ carbons. With a single functional group and forming an ester, T must be an alcohol: ethanol, $\text{CH}_3\text{CH}_2\text{OH}$ shown as $\text{HO-CH}_2\text{-CH}_3$.

Build U as the ester**
Join the acid part to the alcohol part by removing $\text{H}_2\text{O}$: the $\text{OH}$ from S and H from T leave. That gives $$\text{CH}_3\text{CH}_2\text{CH(CH}_3\text{)COOH} + \text{CH}_3\text{CH}_2\text{OH} \rightarrow \text{CH}_3\text{CH}_2\text{CH(CH}_3\text{)COOCH}_2\text{CH}_3 + \text{H}_2\text{O}$$ So U is ethyl 2-methylbutanoate.
